headlines.title: Apple's new foldable iPhone Duo faces ‘Crackgate' controversy amid screen defect reports
headlines.description: The latest star in the Apple phone universe may be losing a little shine. Growing reports indicate that the iPhone Duo, the company’s new foldable phone, is not living up to expectations — specifically, some units are developing cracks where they should not. Apple says it will make good on what some online posters are calling “Crackgate.” While most people interviewed report that their iPhone Duos are working just fine and they are happy with the new product, at least a handful of users say the phones, which start at $2,000, are not ready for prime time. After lining up to get Apple’s first foldable phone, longtime Apple fan Toli Marchuk said he noticed something wrong with his Duo. “First, the selfie camera stopped working; I thought maybe it’ll go away,” Marchuk said. Then came more issues. “I started to get those lines, like people were complaining about, the lines that would kind of pop up, right?” After making a Genius Bar appointment, things got worse. “But then, out of nowhere, it just bricked, it bricked,” he said. Marchuk is not alone. Another user noted issues early in ownership: “I’ve only had the phone a few days; I feel like the hinge shouldn’t be that loose that soon into the life cycle of the phone.” Reports of the phone’s inner screen cracking under strain have led some to dub the controversy “Crackgate.” “It makes people a little bit nervous,” said Matthew Murray, lab director at CNET Labs. Questions remain about how widespread the problem is. Over at CNET Labs, testers have opened and closed a purchased Duo more than 80,000 times. “We haven’t noticed any of that; the phone still looks good; it still opens just as crisply as it did before,” Murray said. Apple released a statement saying, “We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units,” and added that they will replace any defective Duos. Carolina Milanesi, president of Creative Strategies, emphasized the stakes for the company. “These are early adopters, they are the most valuable customers that they have, and they want to make sure they feel taken care of,” Milanesi said. Tech experts note that the situation highlights the importance of getting warranties on expensive devices. For Apple, the issue carries extra weight as it marks the first major product launch under new CEO John Ternus.

headlines.title: San Jose pet owners honor deceased animals with special Día de los Muertos altars
headlines.description: San Jose pet lovers gathered Tuesday to honor the spirits of beloved animals who have passed on during a community-led Día de los Muertos observance. At Unity Bulldogs, a pet grooming business in San Jose, the owner has built an altar so both clients and the community can bring in photos of beloved pets they have lost and honor them. “The sad part is our pets pass away, and these doggies have helped us so much while they were still with us,” said Mario Rodriguez, owner of Unity Bulldogs. Rodriguez built his first altar six years ago, and now dozens of photos are on display. This year, the offering has special meaning because his own dog, Drago, passed away last month. “It definitely helps me heal a lot. He had a good life and he helped me create everything we have today,” Rodriguez said. NBC Bay Area reporter Marianne Favro visited the ofrenda in San Jose to show how pet lovers are paying tribute to their furry family members. “This ofrenda began here at Unity Bulldogs six years ago with just a few photos — you can see here how much it has grown. We consider our pets part of our family, so today I’m honoring my dog Sunny, who recently passed,” Favro said as she placed a photo on the altar. Each photo on the altar represents a beloved pet, best friend, or furry family member. Mario Rodriguez first built the altar years ago for clients, but tonight Drago’s photo is among the many on display. Over the years, the ofrenda grew as clients added photos of the furry friends they have lost. As word spread, the wider community started coming in with photos and other items to honor their dogs and cats as well. “It was nice to see the pictures and reminders of all the good times that people have had with their pets,” said Ezequiel Gatica of San Jose. Across town at a dog park near the SAP Center in San Jose, another tribute to pets will take place tonight. The gathering will include a chance to record a phone message to a dog or cat who has passed. Organizer David Trinh said he believes mourning together as a community can help people heal. “Love is unconditional. And our pets are primary examples of this. The things they do for us go beyond words and they’re only here for a short time,” said David Trinh of RFRD Academy. While their time may be short, it is long enough to leave paw prints on the hearts of those who love them.

headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Napa County California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. Measure B in Napa County: Sales tax to fund wildfire prevention and open space preservation. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Napa County and additional election information, visit the Napa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. headlines.title: Special master could evaluate Justice Department's claims of noncitizens on California voter rolls
headlines.description: A federal judge on Tuesday said he was considering appointing a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that California has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls and to determine whether counties would be able to separate any ballots belonging to ineligible voters. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter was overseeing a hearing in a lawsuit filed by the Justice Department, which is seeking to prevent California from counting ballots from thousands of people it alleges are noncitizens. Carter said it would be too rushed to make a decision without an independent special master who could evaluate the substance of both sides’ claims. He said that could be completed before the state’s Dec. 11 deadline to certify the election results. It is not clear what would happen if a special master did find a substantial number of noncitizen voters on the federal government’s list or whether it would affect the certification of California’s election results. The 20,000 people on the DOJ’s list constitute only a small fraction of California’s 23 million voters. Voting has been well underway for weeks in California in the midterm election that concludes next Tuesday. Alleged voting by noncitizens has been a key focus of President Donald Trump’s administration with control of Congress at stake, though available data indicates occurrences are exceedingly rare. The Republican administration sued election officials in California in mid-October, accusing them of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review its list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls. The Justice Department made a similar request in Washington state this week for the state to sequester ballots submitted by hundreds of people it suspects are not U.S. citizens. Meanwhile, another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent running for U.S. Senate doesn’t win. All three states have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in the nation’s Capitol. Judge issues warning not to threaten election workers Although Carter said he was open to appointing a special master, he said he will not issue an official order until Wednesday. The judge said he wanted to vet the federal government’s list. He emphasized his concerns that siding with the federal government at this stage could mean illegally making substantial changes to election procedure while voting is underway. But he said the special master also could investigate California’s claims that it could not logistically separate the ballots in time for the election certification deadline in December, an assertion the federal government has contested. Carter rarely spoke throughout the hearing, but he did express skepticism about why the federal government was suing California rather than seeking to address alleged noncitizen voting through criminal prosecutions. He referenced the federal government’s recent arrest in October of 28 people across California accused of illegally registering to vote. “You got a remedy for goodness sakes — go out and indict,” Carter said from the bench. Prosecutors with the federal government argued that the U.S. had an interest in preventing noncitizens from voting in the first place. “We want to stop the illegal voting,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said. “We don’t want to chase it later.” Carter also seemed to respond to warnings that local county clerks who don’t heed the federal government’s demands could be criminally prosecuted. “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county election employees cease immediately,” Carter said before abruptly leaving the courtroom. Federal prosecutor says US government seeks to ‘safeguard’ the election Essayli argued Tuesday that the Justice Department’s demands would not significantly disrupt the ongoing election. “We have not asked to void any ballots,” he said. Instead, the government was seeking to work with California officials to “safeguard” the election. He said testimony would explain how the government’s list of 20,000 names was compiled. “The case rises and falls on the credibility” of the flagged names, he told the judge, arguing the state has an obligation to investigate before counting those voters’ ballots. California officials previously argued that once a completed mail ballot is returned, it is separated from the envelope that contains voters’ identification. That would make it impossible to separate ballots that have already been submitted, the state said. More than 3 million ballots have already been returned. Lawyers for California warn of delays and disruptions Lawyers for California and Los Angeles County said the federal government has not specified how or when it obtained the voter file, leaving open the possibility the list was inaccurate or outdated. They specifically questioned the government’s reliance on a private, third-party service to determine Social Security numbers used in their effort. M. Patrick Moore, a lawyer for the Los Angeles County registrar’s office, also argued that the county would cooperate if the federal government wanted to criminally prosecute noncitizens who illegally voted. “If an individual who is a noncitizen votes, there will be record of that, and the county will provide that record” to the federal courts, Moore said in court Tuesday. He added that if the federal government believes the election was compromised, there are legal processes for contesting the outcome. Tuesday’s hearing largely revolved around the reliability of the federal government’s list. Los Angeles County officials found that a small sample of people on it were indeed citizens. The federal agent who conducted the investigation — which required roughly 800 federal employees who manually checked each name — said in an affidavit that the county’s findings were false. The filing did concede that some names of citizens could have been mistakenly included.

headlines.title: East San Jose voting sites change ahead of Election Day
headlines.description: Election Day is one week away, and some voters in East San Jose have learned their voting sites may not be open. Joseph George Middle School, a campus the Alum Rock School District closed last year because of declining enrollment, was going to open on Election Day as a voting center. But over the last few weeks, vandals broke into the school and destroyed classrooms, ripping out cables and electrical wiring and shattering windows. The damage is so bad that the Alum Rock School District told the Registrar of Voters that the school could no longer be a host site for voters next Tuesday. Nearby White Road Baptist Church also recently canceled abruptly. The Registrar of Voters sent affected voters a letter alerting them to the changes and announcing that nearby Latino College Prep Academy will open as an alternative. The Registrar says it is prepared for the change but wants to make sure all voters know about it. “We always have backup vote centers that are available to us, and we want to maintain access to the voters,” Registrar of Voters spokesperson Michael Borja said. As workers continue to count ballots that are already in, the Registrar is reminding voters that there are also roughly 100 secure ballot drop boxes throughout the county, including at libraries. Another 100 early voting centers will open this weekend, including on Halloween.

headlines.title: Election measure on building zoning divides Sausalito
headlines.description: Melissa Pergerson stared at the dilapidated wood paddle wheel rescued from an ancient steam boat, stashed in a forgotten yard in Sausalito’s industrial Marinship neighborhood, and thought back to her childhood. “As a little kid we would play on here and climb up on it,” said Pergerson, who along with her sister Allisandre Haas grew up in Sausalito’s houseboat community. The industrial neighborhood Pergerson now combed through was filled with rotting buildings, many that witnessed the building of Liberty Ships during World War II. Now they served as under-the-radar wood shops, leather works, and artist studios. “This is character,” Pergerson said. “This is history.” Two perspectives of the industrial Marinship are at the center of a contentious battle in Sausalito on the November ballot. Measure X would change zoning laws in the town, allowing building owners to build taller, larger buildings with the possibility of expanded uses such as breweries, cafes and bakeries that can sell to the public on site. It would replace Ordinance 1022, passed by voters in 1985 to regulate development, density, and traffic in industrial areas on the Marinship waterfront, with an eye toward preserving the town’s eccentric character. But many business owners complain the ordinance is preventing them from updating buildings, opening new businesses that can increase revenue, and appeal to a new generation of visitors. “We’re so well known for doing cool things in the 60s and 70s, but we’re not a museum,” said Sharna Brockett, a Sausalito resident who helped write Measure X. “There’s all this new energy that want to do these things, but we’re really holding them back by these laws that were designed for a different time.” Brockett cited longtime local business Heath Ceramics, which she said would have to go to a public vote in order to install a roof on its work yard. She said the business has been beset by king tide floods, which make it difficult to remain in Marinship. “They want to stay here,” Brockett said. “But they don’t know if they’re going to be able to stay here because they can’t make their building more usable.” KC Pederson, the third generation owner of the Clipper Yacht Harbor in Marinship, said Sausalito’s restrictive rules have made it difficult for him and others to install new businesses that can generate enough revenue to pay for upgrades to failing buildings. He said he would love to bring in businesses like coffee shops, bakeries, a retail fish market and maritime retail. But current zoning laws prevent him from doing any of those ideas. “We need mix use, and there’s two sides of that,” Pederson said. “One to bring in more money to sustain that building — also businesses that bring people to the waterfront.” Curtis Havel, the harbormaster of Clipper Yacht Harbor, pointed out a two-story office building on the property. When the top floor became vacant, he and his team envisioned opening a bodega or a craft brewery shop. “While it sounded like a great idea, the answer is no before we even walk through the doors of city hall,” Havel said. But residents like Pergerson worry that Measure X would pave the way for high-end condos and large corporate businesses to take over the waterfront. The measure would extend height limits from the current 32 feet to 47 feet, allowing for three- or possibly four-story buildings. Pergerson and her sister, who own Tile Fever tile shop in Marinship, erected poles on top of their building with streamer lines to designate the current height limit and what it would look like under Measure X. “It changes the character of Sausalito — the Marinship’s plan 1022 was put in place for a reason,” Pergerson said. “To protect the culture, to protect the community, to protect the workers that are here.” Sausalito Councilman Jill Hoffman echoed that concern. She said Measure X would allow new development proposals to pass with the support of three of the city council’s five members. She argued it would usurp environmental controls and other checks and balances from the voters “Anybody can come into city hall the day after this passes and plop down some sort of development plan,” Hoffman said. “And there’s no way for us to say no because there’s no guardrails.” But Brockett said opponents of Measure X have distorted its aims and are fear mongering with the threat of large developments and high-end condos replacing Sausalito’s funky charms. “We don’t want this to be a resort. We don’t want huge buildings here. That’s not what Measure X does,” Brockett said. “We just want to be creative again and have property owners be able to reinvest in their buildings.” Even before the election, Measure X has etched deep divides in the community of 7,000 people. One resident who was job hunting said she feared talking publicly about the measure because she might alienate potential employers. Pergerson walked through a warren of dilapidated Marinship buildings, admiring an old sailing vessel propped up in the yard with its ribs peaking out beneath the rotting wood. While Measure X supporters hold sights like this as a reason to vote for the measure, Pergerson saw it as a reason not to. “I get why they want to change things,” Pergerson said. “But I think the way and their look on it isn’t for all of us.”

headlines.title: 49ers reportedly land DeForest Buckner for fourth-round pick in trade with Colts
headlines.description: The 49ers reunited with a familiar face. San Francisco acquired three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner in a trade with the Indianapolis Colts, NBC Sports Bay Area’s Matt Maiocco confirmed, citing a source, after NFL Media’s Ian Rapoport first reported the news on Tuesday. Rapoport also reported that the 49ers are sending the Colts a 2027 fourth-round draft pick in the deal. The 32-year-old Buckner, who San Francisco selected with the No. 7 pick in the 2016 NFL Draft, spent the first four seasons of his NFL career with the 49ers. He was selected to a Pro Bowl in 2018 before he was traded to Indianapolis for a first-round pick in the 2020 NFL Draft that became defensive tackle Javon Kinlaw. In seven games with the Colts this season, Buckner has 31 combined tackles (11 solo, 20 assisted), four tackles for loss, eight quarterback hits, three passes defensed, one fumble recovery and four sacks. Buckner originally signed a two-year, $46 million contract extension with Indianapolis in April of 2024 and has a $7.9 million salary cap hit this season before he is set to become an unrestricted free agent this upcoming offseason. The 49ers’ defensive line has held up admirably this season in defensive end Nick Bosa’s absence, but another solid pass-rusher and run-stopper like Buckner certainly can elevate the unit as a whole. Now heading into their Week 8 bye, San Francisco will have plenty of time to get Buckner acclimated to new defensive coordinator Raheem Morris’ system before the Week 9 game vs. the Las Vegas Raiders at Levi’s Stadium. headlines.title: High tide flooding causes problems in parts of southern Marin County
headlines.description: For a second straight day, high tides caused problems in parts of southern Marin County. Drivers had to navigate flooded streets. A team of workers had to ditch their cars at their construction site and borrow a boat to grab a bite to eat on their lunch break. A cyclist who rode into San Francisco earlier in the day found his trail underwater when he returned later. “I think this is flooding that we’ve never seen before,” resident Craig Peterson said. “This is an indication of the global warming and climate change. I’ve lived here my whole life, over 50 years, and I’ve never seen flooding like this.” While officials cautioned people about the high tides, some didn’t heed the warnings. One woman had to be rescued when her car stalled in the rising water. A firefighter managed to carry her to safety. bay area weather Oct 26 Severe Weather Oct 20 Roads in Mill Valley that closed due to flooding earlier Tuesday have reopened, police said. Mill Valley police issued an alert around noontime Tuesday advising drivers to avoid Miller Avenue between Camino Alto and Almonte Boulevard, a section of road that runs between Tamalpais High School and the Bothin Marsh Preserve. Also closed was the west side of Redwood Highway, also called Frontage Road, between Hamilton Drive and the on-ramp for southbound Highway 101. Police in an update shortly before 4 p.m. said the flooding had receded and the roadways reopened. The National Weather Service has issued a Coastal Flood Advisory that will be in effect through 5 p.m. Friday for bayshore locations along San Francisco Bay, San Pablo Bay, and Monterey Bay, as well as low-lying areas along the Pacific Coast.
headlines.source: Jodi Hernandez and Ruth Dusseault | Bay City News

headlines.title: Preliminary 2.6 magnitude earthquake strikes near San Jose
headlines.description: A preliminary 2.6 magnitude earthquake struck near San Jose Tuesday afternoon, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 12:38 p.m. and was centered 9 miles east of Seven Trees, 9 miles east-southeast of Alum Rock and 9.8 miles east of Communications Hill, the USGS said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. headlines.title: Risks spelled out for Anthropic investors include blowback from runaway AI
headlines.description: Any time a company looks to start selling shares on Wall Street, it’s required to disclose potential risks to investors. In the case of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic, that has included the possibility that its products could threaten nothing less than humanity itself. The risks laid out by the San Francisco company in its filing Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission included discussion of bad actors potentially using AI models to build deadly weapons or the technology itself going rogue with untold consequences. Of the 335 pages outlining Anthropic’s finances, executive compensation, dividend policy and the like, 93 pages are devoted to “risk factors” — the things that could hurt potential shareholders’ investments. Rival SpaceX’s listed risk factors, in comparison, took up 38 out of more than 250 pages. In selling itself to investors, Anthropic presents its own initial public offering as a step toward mitigating the risks it believes AI poses. “To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” wrote the company’s founders in a letter to prospective shareholders in the IPO filing. “Anthropic is a deeply values-driven organization, founded in large part to help the world realize AI’s benefits and avoid its dangers.” The technology’s potential benefits include leaps in curing diseases and productivity boosts across every sector of the economy, the company said. Still, the potential liabilities are many. They range from the mundane — the possibility it won’t be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — to involvement in cyberattacks and the spread of dangerous misinformation. Here is a look at some of the risks Anthropic details: The technology’s rapid development Anthropic said it’s possible its models could develop so quickly the company won’t be able to implement adequate safety measures, “which could increase the likelihood of safety incidents, regulatory intervention, or reputational harm, and could adversely affect our business.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned in September that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet. The warning — and now Anthropic’s move to sell shares — comes as worries about AI grow inside and outside the industry about increasingly powerful systems that solve problems beyond human capacity but could also act on their own to carry out other, more harmful tasks. As AI systems “become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the SEC filing said, there’s a risk that such systems could “take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” “Even if our own models do not cause such harm, a significant safety incident involving any frontier AI could trigger broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses that could adversely affect our business,” Anthropic said. Now that the AI models are themselves contributing to Anthropic’s own research and development, it’s possible that AI could progress “beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models,” according to the filing. This, the document said, could adversely affect Anthropic’s business. Malicious actors could cause mayhem with the technology The filing discussed concerns that advanced AI systems, if not developed and operated with enough safeguards and oversight, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.” The company said it would be harmed if use by bad actors causes damage, “or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse.” Anthropic sketched out the prospect of bad actors using AI models to build chemical weapons or authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens. In September, the company disclosed that it had blocked efforts to use its AI models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapon development. The company could run up against limits on processing powe r Compute — the computing power or resources needed to build, test and improve AI models — is expensive and in high demand. Anthropic notes that if it’s unable to secure adequate compute, or if “we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers.” Anthropic mentioned community opposition to data centers as a risk to its business. Data center development “has prompted public controversy and regulatory scrutiny regarding environmental impact, land and water use, and the allocation of limited power resources,” the filing said, adding that if regulators impose new requirements or charges as a result, its ability to do business could suffer. In addition, the company relies on a small number of customers, including SpaceX and Microsoft, and distribution channels for a large portion of its revenue. This means that even if just one of its big customers decides to scale back — or drop the company altogether — Anthropic said it could see its prospects and finances suffer. Mitigating the risks In some ways, AI’s enormous risk, combined with its enormous potential, is Anthropic’s main selling point. The company has tried to position itself as a responsible AI company, and courts business customers by emphasizing safety-mindedness. “We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology,” the filing said. Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, said IPO deals have to display “very clearly” what risks people face when they invest their money in a newly public stock. “One of the things that’s great about our capital markets here domestically is the level of transparency that you must commit to, to be a publicly traded corporation on a U.S. exchange requires you to outline those risks in a very clear way, so that people understand if they want to participate by offering their hard-earned money and help finance this type of a deal,” he said. ___ This story has been updated to correct the name of the analyst’s firm to Zacks Investment Management, not Zacks Investment Research. ___ AP Business Writer Bernard Condon and AP Technology Writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed to this story.

headlines.title: Watch: Great white shark cruises by kayak fisherman off Half Moon Bay
headlines.description: David Slavich has spent years enjoying the ocean, but a close encounter with a great white shark near Half Moon Bay last weekend was unlike anything he’s ever experienced out on the water. Slavich was fishing from his kayak on Sunday when the shark approached from behind. “I heard this little splash behind my shoulder,” Slavich told NBC Bay Area. “I look back and I just see this massive fin and shadow. This thing is bigger than my kayak. My kayak’s 12 and a half feet. This thing dwarfed it. Just panic set in.” A camera attached to Slavich captured the entire encounter. “Oh my God. There’s a great white shark,” Slavich can be heard saying. Slavich then repeated “Oh my God” several times as the shark slowly cruised by along the surface of the water. “It was absolutely frightening,” Slavich said. “I think the scariest thing that’s every happened to me in my entire life.” Monterey County Oct 26 Monterey County Oct 19 Despite the scare, Slavich said he stayed out on the water and continued to fish for another three to four hours. “I think like a lot of folks that spend time out on the water here in Northern California or California in general, the boogeyman is the great white shark,” he said. “When you’re surfing, spearfishing, out in the water, it’s just sort of in the back of your mind all the time. Every splash or seagull or anything while I’m out there, I’m hyperaware.” Slavich said he’ll plan to use the buddy system when he heads out on his next ocean adventure. “I need to go with a buddy,” he said. “That’s the safest way to go. I’m not solo kayaking out there any more. That’s one thing I’ll change for sure.”

headlines.title: FBI agent cross-examined in Sheng Thao corruption trial
headlines.description: An FBI agent who investigated former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao for alleged corruption was back on the stand Tuesday in Oakland federal court. FBI Special Agent Katherine Barclay faced a fifth day of testimony as defense attorneys challenged not only her words but also the foundation of the prosecution’s case. Prosecutors allege Thao, her longtime partner Andre Jones, and David and Andy Duong were part of a bribery and corruption scheme to help Thao get elected and siphon money to Jones in exchange for favors to the Duong family, which owns California Waste Solutions, Oakland’s recycling contractor. All four face bribery, fraud and conspiracy charges. Jones’ attorney tried to show the jury Tuesday that Jones was not involved in a corruption and bribery scheme to get Thao elected mayor. During cross-examination, Barclay testified that Jones didn’t respond to a number of texts from businessman Mario Juarez asking for Jones’ thoughts on a negative campaign mailer against Loren Taylor, who ran against Thao. Juarez has pleaded guilty for his role in the alleged scheme, which included producing the mailers in return for favors from Thao when elected mayor. When Jones finally responded to the text, he said that if he helped with the mailer, it would be “coordinating” and that Juarez should run it by someone else. Barclay also testified there are no recorded phone calls with Juarez, which the defense argues is proof Jones didn’t conspire with Juarez. Sheng Thao Oct 26 Sheng Thao Oct 23 Sheng Thao Oct 22 Sheng Thao Oct 13 The defense teams have all argued the so-called deal points listed in text and digital notes between Juarez and Andy Duong never happened. They also claim there’s no proof Thao or Jones knew about any pay-for-play deal. Juarez is expected to testify later on behalf of the prosecution in exchange for a lighter sentence. Before that, Cecilia Mendez, a former California Waste Solutions employee, is expected to testify about secret recordings she made of company meetings. Prosecutors said they plan to play about 40 minutes of audio recordings involving the defendants during Mendez’s testimony.
